name: Odesa Grain Terminal Complex
owner: Multiple operators (Kernel, Cargill, Bunge facilities)
production: ~25 Mt/yr capacity pre-war; handled 50%+ of Ukraine's grain exports
strategic_value: Primary export hub for world's 5th-largest wheat exporter. Russian blockade 2022–23 triggered global food price spike. Black Sea Grain Initiative operated Jul 2022 – Jul 2023 before Russia withdrew.
alert: Under persistent Russian missile/drone threat since Feb 2022. Port infrastructure repeatedly struck after grain deal collapse Jul 2023.

name: Novorossiysk Grain Terminal
owner: Novorossiysk Commercial Sea Port (NCSP) — majority state-controlled via Transneft
production: ~40 Mt/yr grain handling capacity; Russia's largest grain export terminal
strategic_value: Russia became world's largest wheat exporter (~45 Mt in 2023/24 season). Novorossiysk handles the bulk. Gives Moscow leverage over global food prices and dependent importers in MENA/Africa.
alert: Ukrainian naval drone attacks reached Novorossiysk port area in 2023. Insurance costs spiked for Black Sea shipping.

name: Constanta Port Grain Terminal
owner: Constanta Port Authority / multiple private operators
production: ~25 Mt/yr capacity. Volumes surged post-2022 as Ukraine rerouted grain via Danube barges to Constanta.
strategic_value: NATO-member alternative to blocked Ukrainian Black Sea ports. Danube river corridor became critical grain bypass route. EU solidarity lanes channeled Ukrainian grain through Romania.
alert: Capacity bottlenecks and local farmer protests over cheap Ukrainian grain flooding EU markets (2023).

name: US Gulf Grain Export Complex
owner: ADM, Bunge, Cargill, Louis Dreyfus (ABCD traders) + CHS, Zen-Noh
production: ~100+ Mt/yr combined grain/soy exports via Mississippi River system. ~60% of US grain exports transit Gulf ports.
strategic_value: World's largest grain export corridor. Mississippi River low-water crisis (2022) demonstrated vulnerability — barge traffic halted, export delays. Single-point dependency for global food supply.
alert: Climate vulnerability: 2022 drought reduced Mississippi to record lows, disrupting barge traffic for months.

name: Rosario Grain Hub (Up-River Complex)
owner: Cargill, Bunge, COFCO (China), Louis Dreyfus, Viterra (Glencore)
production: ~80 Mt/yr soy/grain capacity. Handles ~80% of Argentina's agricultural exports. World's largest soy crushing cluster.
strategic_value: Argentina is 3rd-largest soy exporter. Parana River drought (2021–22) cut water depth, reducing vessel loads. COFCO (China state) has major terminal presence, securing direct supply chain.
alert: COFCO's growing terminal ownership gives China direct control over South American soy supply chain.

name: Port of Santos — Grain Terminal
owner: Multiple: Cargill, Bunge, COFCO, Louis Dreyfus, Rumo (rail)
production: ~90+ Mt/yr grain/soy throughput. Brazil is world's largest soy exporter (~100 Mt/yr) and a top-5 corn exporter.
strategic_value: Brazil surpassed the US as top soy exporter. Santos is primary outlet. China buys ~70% of Brazil's soy exports. Infrastructure bottlenecks (truck dependency) remain a vulnerability.
alert: Amazon deforestation linked to soy expansion faces EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) restrictions from 2025.

name: Port Kembla Grain Terminal
owner: GrainCorp (ASX-listed)
production: Australia exports ~25-30 Mt/yr wheat (world's 4th-largest exporter). Port Kembla is a key NSW outlet.
strategic_value: Australia's wheat exports critical to SE Asian food security. China imposed unofficial ban on Australian grain (2020–23) during diplomatic rift, then quietly resumed purchases.
alert: China's 2020 trade coercion campaign targeted barley with 80% tariffs; dropped in 2023 as relations thawed.

name: Belaruskali Potash Complex
owner: State-owned (Belaruskali)
production: ~12 Mt/yr potash capacity. Belarus was world's 2nd-largest potash exporter (~20% global supply) before sanctions.
strategic_value: EU/US sanctions (2021 post-election crackdown, expanded 2022) blocked Belaruskali exports via Lithuania's Klaipeda port. Triggered global potash price spike. Developing countries hardest hit.
alert: Sanctions redirected some exports via Russia. Global potash prices tripled 2021–22 before partially normalizing.

name: Nutrien Potash Operations (Saskatchewan)
owner: Nutrien Ltd (world's largest fertilizer company by capacity)
production: ~14+ Mt/yr potash capacity. Canada holds ~30% of global potash reserves. Nutrien is world's largest producer.
strategic_value: Western-aligned potash supply became critical after Belarus/Russia sanctions. Nutrien accelerated expansion to fill gap. Saskatchewan potash is strategic Western fertilizer reserve.

name: Uralkali Potash Operations (Berezniki)
owner: Uralkali (Uralchem group — Dmitry Mazepin, sanctioned)
production: ~11-12 Mt/yr capacity. Russia is world's 3rd-largest potash producer (~18% global).
strategic_value: Combined Russia-Belarus potash (~35-40% global) gives Moscow outsized fertilizer leverage. Sanctions complicated but did not fully halt exports — many developing countries granted exemptions.
alert: Sanctions on owner Mazepin; fertilizer exports partially exempted to prevent global food crisis.

name: OCP Phosphate Mines & Processing (Khouribga/Jorf Lasfar)
owner: OCP Group (state-owned, Kingdom of Morocco)
production: Morocco holds ~70% of global phosphate rock reserves. OCP produces ~40 Mt/yr phosphate rock, ~12 Mt/yr fertilizer products.
strategic_value: Near-monopoly on phosphate reserves makes Morocco a kingmaker in global food security. OCP expanding into Africa with fertilizer plants in Nigeria, Ethiopia. Western Sahara mines remain politically contested.
alert: Western Sahara sovereignty dispute: Polisario Front contests Moroccan extraction. EU court rulings complicate trade agreements.

name: China Phosphate Production (Yunnan/Guizhou/Hubei)
owner: State and private (Yuntianhua Group, Wengfu, Hubei Yihua)
production: ~90 Mt/yr phosphate rock (world's largest producer). China holds ~5% of reserves but mines aggressively.
strategic_value: China imposed phosphate export restrictions (2021-present) to secure domestic food production. Periodic export bans on fertilizer compounds disrupt global markets. Reserves depleting faster than Morocco's.
alert: Recurring export curbs on DAP/MAP fertilizers since Oct 2021 impact SE Asian and South Asian agriculture.

name: TogliattiAzot Ammonia Complex
owner: TogliattiAzot (TOAZ) — Russia's largest ammonia producer
production: ~3 Mt/yr ammonia capacity. Connected to Odesa via 2,400km Togliatti-Odesa ammonia pipeline (world's longest).
strategic_value: Togliatti-Odesa pipeline shut since Feb 2022 war. Was a key global ammonia supply artery. Russia used pipeline restart as leverage in grain deal negotiations. Pipeline damaged by explosion Jun 2023.
alert: Pipeline severed — removing ~2 Mt/yr ammonia from global markets. Contributed to fertilizer price crisis.

name: Point Lisas Industrial Estate — Ammonia/Urea
owner: Multiple: Nutrien, Koch Fertilizer, Yara, NGC (state)
production: ~5 Mt/yr ammonia, ~3.5 Mt/yr urea. World's largest ammonia export site. Supplies ~40% of US nitrogen imports.
strategic_value: Critical Western Hemisphere nitrogen source. Low-cost natural gas feedstock. Reduces US dependency on Russian/Chinese nitrogen. Caribbean location gives short shipping to US Gulf coast.
alert: Aging gas fields threatening feedstock supply. Some plants curtailed due to declining Trinidad gas production.

name: Qatar Fertilizer Company (QAFCO) — Mesaieed
owner: QAFCO (Industries Qatar / Qatar Energy subsidiary)
production: ~3.8 Mt/yr urea capacity (world's largest single-site urea plant). ~2.5 Mt/yr ammonia.
strategic_value: Qatar is world's largest urea exporter. Gas-rich Gulf states dominate nitrogen fertilizer — gives OPEC+ countries dual energy-food leverage.

name: Black Sea Grain Initiative (Collapsed)
owner: UN / Turkey mediation — Russia, Ukraine signatories
production: Enabled ~33 Mt grain exports from Ukraine (Jul 2022 – Jul 2023). Primarily corn, wheat, sunflower products.
strategic_value: Landmark wartime food corridor. Russia withdrew Jul 17, 2023, demanding sanctions relief on own agricultural exports. Collapse spiked wheat prices 8% overnight. Demonstrated food-as-weapon doctrine.
alert: Russia resumed attacking Odesa/Danube port infrastructure within days of withdrawal. No successor agreement as of 2025.

name: Egypt — Wheat Import Dependency
owner: GASC (General Authority for Supply Commodities — state buyer)
production: Imports ~12-13 Mt/yr wheat (world's largest wheat importer). 60%+ came from Russia/Ukraine pre-war.
strategic_value: 100M+ population dependent on subsidized bread. Egypt leverages Suez Canal fees but is hostage to Black Sea grain flows. Shifted to Russian wheat dependency post-2022. Food price spikes risk social instability (cf. 2011 Arab Spring).
alert: Bread subsidies cost ~$3.2B/yr. Suez revenue partially offsets food import bill. Any disruption risks political instability.

name: Horn of Africa Famine Corridor
owner: N/A — humanitarian crisis zone
production: ~50M+ people facing acute food insecurity (IPC 3+) across Horn region as of 2024. Sudan civil war (Apr 2023–) created new famine epicenter.
strategic_value: Intersection of climate drought, conflict, and trade route disruption. Houthi Red Sea attacks (2024) disrupted food aid shipping. Sudan's Port Sudan is contested between warring factions. Region is leverage point for food diplomacy by Russia, Gulf states.
alert: Sudan civil war + Houthi shipping disruption compounding worst food crisis in decades. WFP operations severely hampered.

name: Turkish Straits (Bosporus/Dardanelles) — Grain Control
owner: Republic of Turkey (Montreux Convention 1936 governs transit)
production: ~150 Mt/yr agricultural products transit Turkish Straits. ~12-15% of global seaborne wheat trade passes through.
strategic_value: Turkey controls the sole exit from the Black Sea — world's most important grain waterway. Ankara leveraged this into brokering the grain deal. Montreux Convention gives Turkey wartime closure authority.
alert: Turkey used Montreux to restrict warship transit post-Feb 2022. Grain transit leverage gives Ankara outsized diplomatic weight.

name: China Strategic Grain Reserves (SINOGRAIN)
owner: SINOGRAIN (China Grain Reserves Group — state-owned)
production: Estimated stockpiles: ~50-60% of global wheat reserves, ~60% of global rice reserves, ~70% of global corn reserves (USDA estimates, 2022-23).
strategic_value: China has been aggressively building grain reserves since 2020, holding 18+ months of consumption cover. This distorts global markets and provides massive food security buffer. Policy: 'rice bag' and 'vegetable basket' governors held personally responsible for food supply.
alert: Unprecedented hoarding criticized by WTO members. Reduces global buffer stock available to food-insecure nations.

name: GERD Dam (Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam)
owner: Ethiopian Electric Power (state-owned)
production: 6.45 GW hydroelectric capacity (Africa's largest dam). Reservoir: 74 billion cubic meters. Fifth filling completed 2024.
strategic_value: Controls ~85% of Nile flow to downstream Egypt/Sudan. Egypt views as existential threat to agriculture (Nile irrigates 97% of Egyptian farmland). Decade of failed trilateral negotiations. Ethiopia completed filling unilaterally.
alert: Egypt has repeatedly hinted at military action. Sudan civil war removed a key stakeholder from negotiations. No binding agreement reached.

name: Turkey GAP Dams (Southeastern Anatolia Project)
owner: Turkish State Hydraulic Works (DSI)
production: 22 dams, 19 hydroelectric plants on Tigris-Euphrates system. Ilisu Dam (2020): 1.2 GW, reduced Tigris flow to Iraq by ~50%.
strategic_value: Turkey controls headwaters of Tigris-Euphrates, giving it water leverage over Syria and Iraq. Iraq's agricultural output declined ~40% since 2000 partly due to upstream damming. Weaponization of water flow during droughts.
alert: Iraq declared 2021 water emergency. Basra water crisis displacing farming communities. No binding water-sharing treaty exists.

name: Dalian/Rizhao Soybean Import Terminals
owner: COFCO, Sinograin, Wilmar, Bunge, ADM (crushing facilities)
production: China imports ~100 Mt/yr soybeans (60%+ of global soy trade). Dalian/Rizhao/Nantong handle majority of imports.
strategic_value: China is world's largest soy importer by far, mostly from Brazil/US/Argentina. Feed for 440M pig herd. US-China trade war (2018) showed soy as geopolitical weapon — China shifted purchases to Brazil. Any supply disruption threatens food/feed security.
alert: Over-reliance on imported soy for animal feed. 2018 tariffs on US soy accelerated Brazil deforestation.

name: Bab el-Mandeb Strait — Food Shipping Chokepoint
owner: Contested — Houthi forces control Yemeni side
production: ~7-8 Mt/yr food/grain shipments transit strait. Links Red Sea to Indian Ocean for Suez-bound cargo.
strategic_value: Houthi attacks on commercial shipping (Nov 2023–present) forced major rerouting around Cape of Good Hope. Added 10-14 days and $1M+ per voyage. WFP humanitarian shipments to Yemen/Horn of Africa disrupted. Insurance premiums spiked 10x for Red Sea transit.
alert: Active conflict zone. Rerouting increased food costs to East Africa. Multiple grain carriers targeted since late 2023.

name: India Wheat Export Ban
owner: Government of India — Ministry of Commerce
production: India banned wheat exports in May 2022 after a record heatwave destroyed crops. India is world's 2nd largest wheat producer (~110 Mt/yr) but rarely exports. Ban shocked global markets expecting India to fill Ukraine gap.
strategic_value: Demonstrated that food export bans are contagious — 20+ countries imposed food export restrictions in 2022. India prioritized domestic food security over global supply. Accelerated global food price crisis alongside Ukraine war.
tag: FOOD NATIONALISM — INDIA CHOOSES DOMESTIC OVER GLOBAL
alert: Ban partially lifted in 2023 but restrictions remain on wheat flour and rice exports. India's food nationalism limits its IMEC corridor role as a reliable supply chain partner.

name: Indonesia Palm Oil Export Ban
owner: Government of Indonesia — Ministry of Trade
production: Indonesia banned palm oil exports Apr-May 2022 to control domestic cooking oil prices. Indonesia produces ~60% of global palm oil (~45 Mt/yr). Ban lasted 3 weeks but caused global food industry panic.
strategic_value: Palm oil is in 50% of supermarket products globally. Three-week ban demonstrated Indonesia's leverage over global food supply chains. Malacca Strait nations control critical food commodities alongside trade routes.
tag: PALM OIL WEAPON — MALACCA FOOD LEVERAGE
